subject: embryology
prompt: The right side of the image shows spermatozoa with abnormal head, tail, and size morphology. Which normal process transforms a spermatid into this highly specialized motile cell without another cell division?
explanation: Spermiogenesis is the differentiation of haploid spermatids into spermatozoa. It includes acrosome formation, nuclear condensation, flagellum development, mitochondrial rearrangement, and shedding of residual cytoplasm, but no further cell division.

distractorExplanations.B: Spermatocytogenesis expands and differentiates spermatogonia before the spermatid stage.
distractorExplanations.C: Meiosis I converts a primary spermatocyte into secondary spermatocytes; it does not remodel spermatids.
distractorExplanations.D: Capacitation is a functional change in sperm after ejaculation, not the morphologic production of spermatozoa.

learningObjective: Recognize the morphologic endpoint of spermiogenesis and distinguish it from meiotic division and capacitation.

subject: embryology
prompt: The sequence shows formation of the acrosomal cap during spermiogenesis. Which organelle supplies the vesicles that coalesce into the acrosomal granule?
explanation: Golgi-derived vesicles fuse to form the acrosomal vesicle and granule, which spreads over the anterior nucleus as the acrosomal cap. The centriole contributes to flagellum organization, while mitochondria populate the middle piece.

distractorExplanations.A: Smooth ER is not the source of the acrosomal vesicle.
distractorExplanations.C: Mitochondria reorganize around the proximal flagellum to form the middle-piece sheath.
distractorExplanations.D: The centriole organizes the axoneme; it does not form the acrosomal cap.

learningObjective: Connect the visible acrosomal sequence with its Golgi origin.

subject: embryology
prompt: In the spermatogenic lineage shown, which named cell is the first to be haploid while each chromosome still consists of two sister chromatids?
explanation: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes. Each secondary spermatocyte is therefore haploid, but its chromosomes remain duplicated until sister chromatids separate in meiosis II.

distractorExplanations.A: A type B spermatogonium is diploid and has not entered meiosis.
distractorExplanations.B: A primary spermatocyte has replicated DNA but still contains both homologs of every pair.
distractorExplanations.D: A late spermatid is haploid with single-chromatid chromosomes after meiosis II.

learningObjective: Use the spermatogenic sequence to identify the first haploid cell and its chromosome structure.

subject: embryology
prompt: The sequence shows completion of the first meiotic division and formation of the first polar body. What is normally ovulated?

options.text: A primary oocyte arrested in diplotene of prophase I
A secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II
A mature ovum arrested in anaphase II

acceptedFreeText: A secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II
explanation: The LH surge causes the primary oocyte to complete meiosis I, producing a secondary oocyte and first polar body. The secondary oocyte begins meiosis II and arrests in metaphase II until fertilization.

distractorExplanations.A: The primary oocyte is arrested in prophase I before the preovulatory LH surge, not when normally ovulated.
distractorExplanations.C: The cell becomes a mature ovum only after fertilization triggers completion of meiosis II.
distractorExplanations.D: Oogonia proliferate during fetal life and are not ovulated.

learningObjective: Identify the cell type and meiotic arrest stage present at ovulation.

subject: embryology
prompt: Panel B is dominated by a very large antrum and an eccentrically placed oocyte on the cumulus oophorus. Which follicular stage is this?
explanation: A mature Graafian follicle has a huge fluid-filled antrum and an oocyte displaced to the periphery within the cumulus oophorus. Its wall also contains granulosa and differentiated theca layers.

distractorExplanations.A: A primordial follicle has one layer of flattened follicular cells and no antrum.
distractorExplanations.B: A primary unilaminar follicle has cuboidal follicular cells but no large antrum.
distractorExplanations.C: A preantral follicle has multiple granulosa layers but has not yet developed the dominant antral cavity.

learningObjective: Recognize the defining architecture of a mature Graafian follicle.

subject: embryology
prompt: Comparing panels A and B, what is the earliest visible change as a primordial follicle begins to grow?

options.text: A large antral cavity immediately appears
The theca externa becomes hyaline cartilage

explanation: Activation of a primordial follicle is marked first by enlargement of the oocyte and conversion of the surrounding flattened follicular cells into cuboidal granulosa cells. The zona pellucida then becomes evident as growth proceeds.

distractorExplanations.B: The antrum develops later, after multiple granulosa layers have formed.
distractorExplanations.C: Meiosis II is completed only after fertilization, not during early follicular growth.
distractorExplanations.D: The follicular theca is connective tissue and never becomes cartilage.

learningObjective: Recognize the epithelial change that distinguishes a growing follicle from a primordial follicle.

subject: embryology
prompt: The rightmost panel shows follicles in the newborn ovary. In which stage are the enclosed primary oocytes normally arrested?
explanation: Primary oocytes enter meiosis during fetal life and arrest in diplotene of prophase I. They remain in this dictyate arrest from before birth until recruitment and the preovulatory LH surge years later.

distractorExplanations.A: Oogonia proliferate mitotically earlier in fetal life; newborn primary oocytes have already entered meiosis.
distractorExplanations.C: Metaphase II is the arrest stage of the secondary oocyte after the LH surge.
distractorExplanations.D: Anaphase II occurs only after fertilization initiates completion of meiosis II.

learningObjective: Relate the newborn ovarian image to the prolonged diplotene arrest of primary oocytes.

subject: embryology
prompt: The patient has short stature, a broad shield-like chest, and poor development of secondary sexual characteristics. Which karyotype best fits this phenotype?
explanation: Turner syndrome is monosomy X, classically 45,X. Typical findings include short stature, a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, gonadal dysgenesis, and failure of normal pubertal development.

distractorExplanations.B: 47,XXY causes Klinefelter syndrome in a phenotypic male, usually with tall stature and small testes.
distractorExplanations.C: Trisomy 21 produces Down syndrome rather than this gonadal-dysgenesis phenotype.
distractorExplanations.D: 46,XX is a normal female karyotype and does not explain the syndrome.

learningObjective: Recognize the characteristic body habitus of Turner syndrome and match it to monosomy X.

subject: embryology
prompt: The patient is a tall phenotypic male with long limbs, sparse body hair, small testes, and gynecomastia. Which karyotype is most likely?

distractorExplanations.C: 47,XYY does not classically cause the hypogonadism and gynecomastia shown.

subject: embryology
prompt: The newborn shows clenched hands with overlapping fingers and a rocker-bottom configuration of the feet. Which chromosomal abnormality is most strongly associated with this pattern?
explanation: Edwards syndrome is trisomy 18. Classic findings include clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, growth restriction, a prominent occiput, and severe congenital anomalies.

distractorExplanations.A: Trisomy 13 is more strongly associated with holoprosencephaly, cleft lip or palate, and polydactyly.
distractorExplanations.C: Trisomy 21 classically causes hypotonia, characteristic facial features, a single transverse palmar crease, and congenital heart disease.
distractorExplanations.D: Monosomy X causes Turner syndrome and does not produce this neonatal anomaly pattern.

learningObjective: Distinguish the characteristic limb findings of Edwards syndrome from other aneuploidies.

subject: embryology
prompt: The image shows a newborn with the typical facial appearance of Down syndrome and a hand with a single transverse palmar crease. Which karyotype is the most common underlying abnormality?
explanation: Most Down syndrome results from free trisomy 21 due to meiotic nondisjunction, producing 47 chromosomes with an extra chromosome 21. A minority results from Robertsonian translocation or mosaicism.

distractorExplanations.B: Trisomy 18 causes Edwards syndrome with a different anomaly pattern.

learningObjective: Match the characteristic Down syndrome phenotype with the common trisomy 21 karyotype.

subject: embryology
prompt: Inspect the karyotype: chromosome 21 is present in three copies, and two X chromosomes are present. Which notation is correct?

subject: embryology
prompt: The diagram shows fusion of the long arms of chromosomes 14 and 21 into a balanced Robertsonian translocation. How many chromosomes does an unaffected balanced carrier usually have?
explanation: A balanced Robertsonian carrier has 45 chromosomes because two acrocentric chromosomes have fused into one derivative chromosome. The important long-arm genetic material is balanced, so the carrier is usually phenotypically normal but has reproductive risk.

distractorExplanations.A: Only one net chromosome is lost from the count, not two.
distractorExplanations.C: The usual balanced carrier count is 45 because the fused derivative is counted as one chromosome.
distractorExplanations.D: Forty-seven chromosomes would suggest a supernumerary chromosome rather than a balanced carrier.

learningObjective: Relate Robertsonian fusion to the characteristic 45-chromosome count in a balanced carrier.

subject: embryology
prompt: In panel B, homologous chromosomes fail to separate during the first meiotic division. What gamete pattern results after meiosis II?

options.text: Two normal gametes, one n+1 gamete, and one n−1 gamete
Two n+1 gametes and two n−1 gametes
One diploid gamete and three normal gametes

acceptedFreeText: Two n+1 gametes and two n−1 gametes
explanation: When homologs fail to separate in meiosis I, both products are abnormal. After meiosis II, two gametes carry an extra chromosome and two lack that chromosome; no normal gametes are produced.

distractorExplanations.A: That pattern is associated with meiosis II nondisjunction, where two gametes remain normal.
distractorExplanations.B: Meiosis I nondisjunction makes every resulting gamete aneuploid.
distractorExplanations.D: The products differ by one chromosome, not by an entire haploid set.

learningObjective: Distinguish the gamete pattern produced by meiosis I nondisjunction from meiosis II nondisjunction.

subject: embryology
prompt: The diagram contrasts female and male maturation divisions. Why does one primary oocyte usually yield only one functional gamete while one primary spermatocyte yields four?

options.text: Oogenesis uses unequal cytokinesis that preserves cytoplasm in one cell
The primary oocyte skips meiosis I
Spermatocytes undergo two extra mitotic divisions after meiosis II
Polar bodies receive all maternal chromosomes

acceptedFreeText: Oogenesis uses unequal cytokinesis that preserves cytoplasm in one cell
explanation: Oocyte maturation uses highly unequal cytokinesis, retaining nearly all cytoplasm in one large ovum while small polar bodies dispose of the extra chromosome sets. Spermatogenesis partitions cytoplasm much more evenly among four spermatids.

distractorExplanations.B: The primary oocyte completes meiosis I before ovulation.
distractorExplanations.C: The four spermatids are the direct products of meiosis; no two extra mitoses are required.
distractorExplanations.D: Polar bodies receive chromosomes but not all maternal chromosomes; the ovum remains haploid.

learningObjective: Explain the unequal functional output of oogenesis and spermatogenesis from the visible maturation pattern.

subject: embryology
prompt: Panel C shows a chiasma between paired homologous chromosomes. Which event produced the recombinant chromatids seen later in the sequence?

options.text: Crossing over between nonsister chromatids during pachytene
Independent replication of centromeres during metaphase II
Fusion of sister chromatids during anaphase I

acceptedFreeText: Crossing over between nonsister chromatids during pachytene
explanation: During pachytene of prophase I, nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange corresponding DNA segments. Chiasmata are the visible manifestations of those crossover sites as homologs begin to separate.

distractorExplanations.B: DNA replication precedes meiosis I; centromere replication in metaphase II does not generate recombination.
distractorExplanations.C: Homologs separate in anaphase I, but sister chromatids do not fuse.
distractorExplanations.D: The recombinant chromatids are generated during meiotic prophase I before fertilization.

learningObjective: Recognize a chiasma and connect it to crossing over between nonsister chromatids in pachytene.

subject: embryology
prompt: The image places primordial germ cells temporarily in the yolk-sac wall near the allantois. Where must these cells migrate to establish the future gonads?

options.text: Genital ridges on the posterior abdominal wall
Surface ectoderm of the genital tubercle

acceptedFreeText: Genital ridges on the posterior abdominal wall
explanation: Primordial germ cells are first identifiable in the yolk-sac wall near the allantois. They migrate along the dorsal mesentery of the hindgut to the genital or gonadal ridges, where they populate the developing gonads.

distractorExplanations.B: External genital ectoderm is not the destination of primordial germ-cell migration.
distractorExplanations.C: The septum transversum contributes to diaphragm and liver-associated structures, not the germ-cell destination.
distractorExplanations.D: The neural tube does not receive primordial germ cells.

learningObjective: Trace primordial germ cells from the yolk-sac wall to the gonadal ridges.

subject: histology
prompt: This low-power field is dominated by branching eosinophilic trabeculae separated by marrow spaces rather than concentric osteons. Which tissue is being shown?
explanation: Spongy bone is organized as a three-dimensional network of trabeculae with intervening marrow spaces. Compact bone instead forms dense lamellae arranged around Haversian canals as osteons.

distractorExplanations.A: Compact bone is dense and typically displays osteons rather than broad interconnected marrow spaces.
distractorExplanations.C: Hyaline cartilage has chondrocytes in lacunae within a glassy matrix, not trabeculae around marrow.
distractorExplanations.D: Dense regular connective tissue forms parallel collagen bundles without mineralized trabeculae.

learningObjective: Distinguish cancellous bone from compact bone and cartilage at low magnification.

media.alt: Low-power microscope photograph of branching bone trabeculae and marrow spaces
media.attribution: TUMS MD&MBBS TERM 2 Telegram, Histology1 topic

subject: histology
prompt: The low-power field shows opposing articular surfaces separated by a true joint cavity and surrounded by a capsule. Which class of joint is this?
explanation: A synovial joint has a real cavity between articular surfaces, hyaline articular cartilage, a fibrous capsule, and an inner synovial lining. Fibrous and cartilaginous joints do not contain a synovial cavity.

distractorExplanations.A: A fibrous suture joins bones with dense connective tissue and has no joint cavity.
distractorExplanations.B: A synchondrosis is united by hyaline cartilage without a synovial space.
distractorExplanations.C: A symphysis is united by fibrocartilage and lacks a true synovial cavity.

learningObjective: Recognize a synovial joint from its low-power architecture.
